summary.text: Letting \(x=a(6)=(2^{171}+1)/9\), reduction of \(9x=2^{171}+1\) modulo \(81\), together with parity, gives \(x\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Hence \(2^x\equiv2^3=8\pmod{19}\), so \(2^x+1\equiv9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\); since \(19\mid171=a(5)\), the division required to form \(a(7)\) is not exact.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by showing that the recurrence first fails to produce an integer at the seventh term.

The recurrence is
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
Its first few terms are obtained directly:
\[
a(3)=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,
\]
\[
a(4)=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,
\]
and
\[
a(5)=\frac{2^9+1}{3}=\frac{513}{3}=171.
\]
Thus the sixth term, if integral, is
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
Define
\[
N:=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
We first check that this really is an integer. Modulo \(9\), one has
\[
2^6=64\equiv1\pmod 9.
\]
Since \(171=6\cdot28+3\), it follows that
\[
2^{171}\equiv 2^3=8\equiv-1\pmod 9.
\]
Therefore \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\), so \(N\) is a positive integer and
\[
9N=2^{171}+1. \tag{1}
\]
Consequently the recurrence is well-defined over the integers through \(a(6)=N\).

We next determine the residue of \(N\) modulo \(18\). For this, first compute the right-hand side of (1) modulo \(81\). We have
\[
2^9=512\equiv26\pmod{81}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv26^2=676\equiv28\pmod{81},
\]
and hence
\[
2^{27}=2^{18}2^9\equiv28\cdot26=728\equiv-1\pmod{81},
\]
because \(728=9\cdot81-1\). Since \(171=6\cdot27+9\), we obtain
\[
2^{171}=(2^{27})^6 2^9\equiv(-1)^6\cdot26=26\pmod{81}.
\]
It follows from (1) that
\[
9N=2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{81}. \tag{2}
\]
Write \(N=9q+r\), where \(0\le r<9\). Then
\[
9N\equiv9r\pmod{81}.
\]
Together with (2), this gives \(9r\equiv27\pmod{81}\). Both \(9r\) and \(27\) lie between \(0\) and \(72\), so they must be equal. Thus \(r=3\), and therefore
\[
N\equiv3\pmod 9. \tag{3}
\]

Moreover, the right-hand side of (1) is odd: \(2^{171}\) is even, so \(2^{171}+1\) is odd. Since \(9\) is odd and \(9N\) is odd, \(N\) itself is odd. Combining this with (3) determines its residue modulo \(18\). Indeed, write \(N=9q+3\). Because \(N\) is odd, \(9q+3\) is odd, which forces \(q\) to be even. Hence \(q=2t\) for some integer \(t\), and
\[
N=18t+3.
\]
Thus
\[
N\equiv3\pmod{18}. \tag{4}
\]

Now consider the putative seventh term. The recurrence would give
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}= rac{2^N+1}{171}.
\]
For this to be an integer, it would be necessary that
\[
171\mid 2^N+1. \tag{5}
\]
We show that (5) is impossible by reducing modulo \(19\). Since
\[
171=9\cdot19,
\]
condition (5) would imply
\[
2^N+1\equiv0\pmod{19}. \tag{6}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
2^9=512=19\cdot27-1,
\]
so
\[
2^9\equiv-1\pmod{19}
\quad\text{and consequently}\quad
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}.
\]
Using (4), write \(N=18t+3\). Then
\[
2^N=2^{18t+3}=(2^{18})^t2^3\equiv1^t\cdot8=8\pmod{19}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^N+1\equiv9\pmod{19},
\]
which is not congruent to \(0\) modulo \(19\). This contradicts (6). Hence
\[
171\nmid 2^N+1.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^N+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer, even though all preceding terms \(a(1),\ldots,a(6)\) are integers. Therefore the conjecture that every term of A078590 is an integer is false.
